angle: No seat limits, purely usage-based, and a 20-person team: why a full sales process on every signup is impossible
linkedin_post:
20-something people. Endless signups.

Dima Khlopkov's team hit a wall that no sales process could solve.

The volume of incoming signups and leads was far too high for a team that lean. Running a full sales process on every one of them was simply impossible.

So about 4 months ago, maybe 5, the approach changed. There are no limits now. Pricing is purely usage-based.

Dima described the result as a hybrid approach: the product handles the volume, and the team's time goes where it matters.

The lesson for lean teams: if your headcount can't scale with signups, your pricing and motion have to.

How does your team handle signup volume?

Slide 2: Signups and leads kept coming in at high volume.
Slide 3: A full sales process on every signup was impossible.
Slide 4: So about 4 months ago, the model changed.
Slide 5: No limits. Purely usage-based pricing.
Slide 6: The result is a hybrid approach to go-to-market.
Slide 7: Lean teams must match their motion to their capacity.

lesson.title: Build a go-to-market motion your headcount can support
takeaways: When signup volume outgrows a roughly 20-person team, a full sales process on every lead stops being possible.
Usage-based pricing with no limits lets the product carry volume that sales can't.
A hybrid approach lets a lean team focus human effort selectively instead of evenly.
lesson.exercise: Count your monthly signups, then estimate how many your team can realistically run a full sales process on. Decide what happens to the rest.

angle: From easy to hard PLG signals: from 30-day inactivity to a power user who changes jobs and champions you at the new company
post_first_line: 30 days inactive is your easiest PLG signal.
linkedin_post:
30 days inactive is your easiest PLG signal.

The hardest one is a lot more valuable.

Dima Khlopkov, who works on growth at Gumloop, breaks PLG signals into a spectrum. On the simple end: someone goes quiet for around 30 days, then logs back in.

On the hard end: a power user switches jobs, lands in a new workspace, and starts trying out Gumloop, even on a free package.

That second signal is tough to catch. But it means someone who already knows the product might champion it inside a new org, and they'll likely be more excited when someone reaches out.

Dima's advice on where to start: don't overthink signals.

Implement whatever comes to mind first. Then iterate across different places and sequences as you learn.

The spectrum runs from simple to advanced. You don't need the advanced ones to begin.

What's the first PLG signal you'd set up?

Slide 2: Easy signal: a user inactive for about 30 days logs back in.
Slide 3: Hard signal: a power user changes jobs and joins a new workspace.
Slide 4: They try the product again, even on a free package.
Slide 5: Reaching out then means a warmer, more excited conversation.
Slide 6: That person can champion you inside the new org.
Slide 7: Don't overthink signals. Ship the first ones that come to mind.
Slide 8: Then iterate across places and sequences over time.

lesson.title: Start Simple With PLG Signals, Then Climb the Ladder
takeaways: PLG signals range from simple (30-day inactivity then a login) to advanced (a power user showing up at a new company).
A former power user who restarts at a new org can become a champion there, and is likely to be more excited about outreach.
Overthinking signals is a mistake. Implement what comes to mind first, then iterate across places and sequences.

angle: A 3-tier outbound system: manual for top accounts, semi-automated in the middle, fully automated for the rest
post_first_line: Three tiers. Three levels of automation.
linkedin_post:
Three tiers. Three levels of automation.

Dima Khlopkov shared how the Unify team splits outbound so effort matches account value.

Tier 1 is the most manual. The GTM team writes the emails by hand and refines them. Sometimes there's a link between our head of sales or a founder and that individual. That detail is not obvious and impossible to gather with an AI agent and a web search.

Tier 2 is semi-automated. Emails are automated, but LinkedIn steps stay manual. The goal is to diversify how those accounts get touched.

Tier 3 is a fully automated sequence.

The point is not to automate everything. It's to spend human time only where a human adds something a workflow can't.

Which tier does most of your pipeline come from?
carousel: Slide 1: Not every account deserves the same outbound effort.
Slide 2: Split your outbound into three tiers.
Slide 3: Tier 1: manual emails, refined by your GTM team.
Slide 4: Use personal links between your leaders and the prospect.
Slide 5: An AI agent with web search can't find those.
Slide 6: Tier 2: automated emails, manual LinkedIn steps.
Slide 7: Tier 3: a fully automated sequence.
Slide 8: Spend human time only where it changes the outcome.

lesson.title: Match outbound effort to account tier
takeaways: Tier 1 accounts get manual emails, so personal connections can be mentioned that an AI agent and web search would miss.
Tier 2 accounts mix automated emails with manual LinkedIn steps to diversify touchpoints.
Tier 3 accounts run on a fully automated sequence.
lesson.exercise: Sort your target account list into three groups. For each, decide which steps stay manual and which are automated. Then look for one personal connection between your leadership and each tier 1 account.

angle: Timing beats messaging: reach people the week they try your product, and name-drop a teammate
post_first_line: Timing beats messaging at every level.
linkedin_post:
Timing beats messaging at every level.

Dima Khlopkov thinks most teams are optimizing the wrong variable.

Dima's reasoning: when someone just tried Gumloop, they're excited about the platform. That's the best state possible to start a conversation.

So the message doesn't need to be clever. Dima keeps it very simple.

Personalize based on role. GTM teams are using Gumloop for this and that. Marketing teams are using it for this and that.

Then add one more layer: name-drop people.

In Dima's opinion, that's a different level of personalization. You can't really source that information from the internet.

The order of operations is the lesson. Reach out the week someone tries the product, keep the copy plain, and let a familiar name do the heavy lifting.

Where do you put more effort: timing or copy?
carousel: Slide 1: Timing beats messaging at every level.
Slide 2: Someone who just tried your product is excited right now.
Slide 3: That's the best state to start a conversation.
Slide 4: Keep the message simple. Personalize by role.
Slide 5: GTM teams use us for this. Marketing teams for that.
Slide 6: Then name-drop a teammate or someone they know.
Slide 7: That level of personalization can't be sourced online.
Slide 8: Fix when you reach out before you rewrite what you say.

lesson.title: Timing first, then a name drop
takeaways: People who just tried your product are at peak excitement, so that's the best moment to reach out.
A simple message personalized by role is enough when timing is right.
Name-dropping people is a deeper kind of personalization because that information can't be found on the internet.
lesson.exercise: Pick the last 10 people who tried your product this week. Write one short role-based message for each, include one name drop of someone relevant, and send within days of their trial.

angle: 10-12% reply rates from acting on one LinkedIn signal: who viewed your founder's profile
linkedin_post:
10 to 12% reply rates from outbound.

The trigger behind it is surprisingly simple.

Dima Khlopkov noticed that when a prospect recently viewed the founder's profile, viewed the company profile, or engaged with the company's content, Gumloop was top of mind for them.

That's the best time to reach out.

The approach combines inbound and outbound without being pushy. The outreach just lands at the right moment.

Dima found the team can keep 10 to 12% reply rates by acting on LinkedIn-based signals and keeping inbound-led outbound flows.

The signal isn't a bigger list or a cleverer subject line. It's knowing who already raised a hand, even quietly.

angle: What's a good positive reply rate? Product signals can run 4x the norm
post_first_line: Product signals can beat typical reply rates 4x.
linkedin_post:
Product signals can beat typical reply rates 4x.

But the answer to "what's a good positive reply rate" starts with "it depends."

Quintin Smith has been digging into this data at Unify. The honest answer is that reply rate is determined by the type of signal behind the outreach. It also keeps climbing as signals get combined and layered.

Here's the range Quintin shared:

- Positive replies: anywhere from 0.2 to 1%
- Standard replies overall: 1 to 3%

Then there's the outlier. For product signals specifically, the reply rate can be 4x higher than a typical positive reply rate.

The reason is simple. Those are your warmest accounts. They're already using the product.

So a benchmark without the signal type attached doesn't tell you much. A 1% positive reply rate on cold outreach and a 1% on product signal outreach are two very different results.

What's your best-performing signal type right now?
carousel: Slide 1: What's a good positive reply rate? It depends.
Slide 2: Reply rate is driven by the type of signal.
Slide 3: Layering and combining signals pushes it higher.
Slide 4: Positive replies often land between 0.2 and 1%.
Slide 5: Standard replies tend to run 1 to 3%.
Slide 6: Product signals can hit 4x a typical positive reply rate.
Slide 7: Those are your warmest accounts, already in the product.
Slide 8: Benchmark by signal type, not one blended number.

lesson.title: Stop Benchmarking Reply Rates Without Signal Type
takeaways: Positive reply rate depends heavily on the signal behind the outreach, so one blended benchmark misleads.
Typical ranges: 0.2 to 1% for positive replies, 1 to 3% for standard replies.
Product signals can run about 4x a typical positive reply rate because they surface your warmest accounts.
lesson.exercise: Split last quarter's outbound by signal type (product, other signals, no signal) and calculate positive reply rate for each. Compare the gap to the 4x benchmark.
